title: Data Ownership and Distributed Transactions
subtitle: Make ownership and consistency explicit
summary: Once data is separated, every table needs an owner and every multi-service update needs a consistency strategy. Single ownership assigns writes to the service that naturally controls a table. Common ownership introduces a dedicated owner for data used by several services. Joint ownership can be resolved through table splitting, a shared data domain, delegation to one preferred owner, or service consolidation. These choices trade autonomy, coupling, security, and operational complexity. A distributed transaction cannot provide the same single ACID unit of work as local tables, so eventual consistency patterns become necessary. Background synchronization is simple but tightly coupled to data sources; orchestrated request-based coordination makes steps explicit but leaves difficult failure handling; event-based coordination decouples participants but requires durable events, idempotent consumers, and observability. The chapter’s decision process favors explicit ownership and measured trade-offs, with delegation often preserving a tight owner boundary while allowing another service to request changes.

concepts.title: Assign an owner
concepts.body: Single ownership gives one service authority over writes and therefore a clear bounded context. Common ownership creates a dedicated service when several domains need the same table. Joint ownership occurs when multiple services write the same table and must be resolved deliberately. Read access is a separate concern; ownership primarily means responsibility for mutations and integrity.
concepts.example: Catalog owns product descriptions while Inventory requests changes through Catalog. An audit table used by many services can instead belong to an Audit service fed by messages.

concepts.title: Resolve joint writes
concepts.body: Table split separates fields or records so each service owns a smaller table, but requires restructuring and synchronization. A shared data domain preserves joins and constraints while broadening the context. Delegation assigns a table to one service based on domain priority or operational characteristics and routes other writes through it. Consolidation combines services when the shared transaction or workflow outweighs independent deployment.
concepts.example: Catalog and Inventory both write product data. Delegation can make Catalog the owner and have Inventory submit stock updates, preserving one table while exposing the dependency through an API.

concepts.title: Local versus distributed
concepts.body: A local transaction can commit or roll back several writes atomically. After data is split, remote calls create separate commits; a later failure can leave participants inconsistent. The architecture must therefore state what temporary inconsistency is acceptable and how repair, retries, and user-visible status work. Distributed boundaries are not free substitutes for ACID guarantees.
concepts.example: An unsubscribe request may remove a profile immediately while contract and billing records catch up. The system needs a durable signal and a way to detect and repair missing updates.

concepts.title: Eventual consistency patterns
concepts.body: Background synchronization periodically compares sources and repairs secondary data but couples the synchronizer to schemas. Orchestrated request-based consistency uses a coordinator to call participants in sequence, making workflow visible but complicating timeouts and partial failure. Event-based consistency publishes a domain event and lets subscribers react independently, improving decoupling while requiring durable delivery, idempotency, ordering decisions, and monitoring.
concepts.example: Customer Profile publishes CustomerUnsubscribed. Contract and Billing consume it and record processing status; replay handles a consumer outage without forcing the profile service to call both synchronously.

misconceptions.claim: Every table should have exactly one service and no shared data is ever acceptable.
misconceptions.correction: Single ownership is a useful default, but common ownership, shared domains, delegation, or consolidation can fit the actual transaction and domain forces.

misconceptions.claim: Eventual consistency means the system can ignore failed updates.
misconceptions.correction: It requires explicit events, retries or replay, idempotent handling, and observability so temporary divergence can converge.

scenario.title: Unsubscribe across domains
scenario.context: A customer profile, support contract, and billing service each store subscription state. Customers expect the profile screen to confirm quickly, but billing must eventually stop charges. The services deploy independently and cannot share a database transaction. Choose a coordination pattern with a recoverable failure path.

options.label: Orchestrate
options.benefit: One coordinator can track each response and show a workflow outcome.
options.cost: The coordinator accumulates coupling and must handle timeouts, retries, and partial completion.
options.consequence: Profile calls Contract and Billing in sequence. A billing timeout leaves a visible pending state and demands durable workflow state plus compensating or retry behavior.

options.label: Publish event
options.benefit: Subscribers remain decoupled and can process independently or replay after outages.
options.cost: The profile response precedes downstream completion, and correctness depends on durable delivery and idempotent consumers.
options.consequence: Profile commits removal and publishes CustomerUnsubscribed. Contract and Billing consume it, expose lag metrics, and replay from the stream when a consumer falls behind.

scenario.debrief: The user-facing timing and failure model determine the choice. Orchestration offers immediate coordination visibility; events offer stronger decoupling. Either requires an explicit state model and recovery evidence.

quiz.question: What does data ownership primarily govern?
options: Which service may write and protect a table
Which service may cache any response
quiz.explanation: Ownership is about mutation authority and integrity responsibility; read access can be designed separately.

quiz.question: Why can’t separated writes share one local ACID transaction?
options: Remote calls commit in separate transactional units
quiz.explanation: A distributed call can succeed in one participant and fail in another, so atomic rollback is no longer automatic.

quiz.question: Which pattern best supports replay after a subscriber outage?
options: A direct SQL join across services
quiz.explanation: Durable events can be replayed by idempotent consumers; direct joins violate ownership and an undocumented script hides coupling.

exercise.title: Define ownership and convergence
exercise.prompt: Model a workflow that updates data in two or more services. Assign table owners, choose orchestration or events, and specify retries, idempotency, user-visible state, and a repair signal.

fields.label: Trade-off
fields.placeholder: Failure, latency, coupling, and recovery consequences

steps.text: Identify every service that mutates the shared business fact and the transaction it expects.
Assign one owner or choose a deliberate joint-ownership resolution technique.
Publish an explicit change signal when a distributed update must converge.
Retry, replay, and measure lag or divergence until all participants reach the intended state.
